analyzedSources.bodySummary: Defines combination skin as oily or normal in some places and dry in others, then structures care around cleanse, treat and moisturise.
Frames combination skin as mixed oiliness and dryness but moves immediately into shopping categories, exposing a product-first SERP pattern.
Describes combination skin as a varied face rather than a fixed fifty-fifty split and proposes area-based care with dermatologist escalation.
Emphasises that skin and routine needs shift with age and weather and that no single short routine works for everyone.
Provides an India-market product routine, illustrating demand for a simple step sequence but remaining commercially specific.
Uses a simple routine and warns that heavy textures may be unsuitable for skin that tends to be oily in some areas.
Applies combination-skin language to Indian climate and seasonal changes but makes broad causal claims and product recommendations to avoid repeating.
Promotes a simple, consistent routine and highlights reader uncertainty between midday oiliness and dry or dull-feeling cheeks.
Supplies general guidance on individual cleansing needs, moisturiser textures, sun protection and caution around combining active ingredients.
Uses skin type as a layering context and reinforces that readers arrive looking for a clear sequence more than a complicated routine.

gaps: SERP pages usually jump straight to products.
India-specific content can overstate climate mechanisms.
Few help readers decide which facial areas need different attention without complexity.
differentiationOpportunities: Lead with a three-step baseline instead of product shopping.
Make seasonal flexibility and medical boundaries explicit.

judgmentChecks.notes: Ten sources were read for page hierarchy, claims and gaps; the final page uses an original zones-first, non-diagnostic approach.
